title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A robot is not a novelty gadget; it is an economic machine designed to reduce human error, compress labor costs, and operate without fatigue.
epigraph.author: Analyst's field notebook

web_blocks.text: Kody Technolab operates across two distinct operational verticals that reflect its past roots and future ambitions. Specifically, (1) Robotics Hardware, Autonomous Systems & Kody OS Solutions. (2) Enterprise Software Development, AI Platforms & Digital Consulting. In FY26, consolidated revenue from operations reached ₹80.00 crore. Based on company filings, management commentary. Segment disclosures, the robotics and autonomous systems vertical contributed approximately 68% of consolidated top-line revenue (roughly ₹54.40 crore). Meanwhile, legacy enterprise IT services and digital transformation contributed the remaining 32% (approximately ₹25.60 crore). Geographically, domestic Indian commercial deployments accounted for roughly 62% of revenue. This comes with international projects (primarily UAE/GCC and early North American customer engagements) contributing 38%. [1][3][8]

web_blocks.takeaway: Robotics is now the dominant revenue driver (~68% of sales), but it carries heavy working capital demands compared to the legacy IT services engine (~32% of sales). [1][3]

web_blocks.text: To understand the robotics vertical, one must examine its core commercial product families. Specifically, (1) Odigo is an autonomous indoor advertising, navigation. Customer engagement robot featuring twin vertical high-definition touch displays, voice interaction, facial recognition for demographic audience analytics. Programmatic ad scheduling. It is designed to navigate crowded retail concourses, guide shoppers to specific storefronts. Generate advertising revenue. (2) Dasher is an autonomous hospitality service robot built with a three-tier tray structure, a 40 kg payload capacity, LiDAR-based SLAM navigation. Dynamic obstacle avoidance. This enables food and beverage delivery in restaurants, corporate cafeterias. Hotels. (3) Athena is an autonomous security patrol robot featuring 360-degree cameras, thermal vision, night-vision infrared sensors, unattended object detection. Automated perimeter route patrolling. (4) Vulcan represents Kody's industrial Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) family, engineered for factory intralogistics, material movement. Warehouse pallet transfer with payloads up to 1,000 kg. [2][8][9]

A rigorous institutional monograph requires concrete, end-to-end operational walkthroughs of how these machines are procured, deployed. Monetized in the real world. Below are detailed walkthroughs covering Kody's primary product lines across hospitality, retail media. Perimeter security. [2][3]

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 1: Odigo Programmatic Advertising & Concierge Robot in GCC Retail
paragraphs: Customer and Problem. Specifically, A premier luxury shopping mall operator or digital-out-of-home (DOOH) advertising media agency in Dubai (such as partner Hypermedia FZ-LLC or Falcon Tech Robotics) seeks to capture consumer attention in sprawling atrium concourses where static billboards suffer from banner blindness. Meanwhile, simultaneously providing automated indoor wayfinding for visitors.

Bought Solution. Specifically, A fleet of 10 Kody Odigo autonomous advertising and concierge robots equipped with Kody OS, dual 27-inch vertical 4K touch displays, 360-degree LiDAR, depth-sensing cameras. Programmatic cloud ad-exchange software.

Engineering and Delivery Workflow. Specifically, Kody's Gandhinagar plant fabricates the reinforced aluminum-composite chassis, mounts brushless drive motors and omnidirectional wheels, integrates NVIDIA Jetson compute units and solid-state LiDAR sensors. Loads Kody OS. The robots are shipped to Dubai. On-site field engineers conduct an initial SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) lidar survey of the mall floorplan, defining virtual keep-out zones (escalators, water features) and programming high-footfall patrol routes between anchor retail stores.

Monetization and Pricing. Specifically, The commercial transaction operates via a hybrid capital equipment and software model. Specifically, hardware sale at approximately ₹15–20 lakh ($18,000–$24,000) per unit, plus an ongoing annual cloud telemetry and software maintenance fee of ₹1.5–2.0 lakh ($2,000) per robot. The media agency monetizes the robot by selling targeted 15-second dynamic video ad slots to mall retailers (fashion brands, jewelers, restaurants), utilizing Odigo's audience analytics to report impression counts, dwell times. Demographic engagement to advertisers.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 2: Dasher Autonomous Food & Beverage Runner in Commercial Hospitality
paragraphs: Customer and Problem. Specifically, A 250-seat banquet hall and multi-cuisine restaurant in Ahmedabad faces acute server shortages, high waiter turnover. Slow food expediting during peak dinner rushes. This leads to cold food delivery and customer dissatisfaction.
Bought Solution. Specifically, Two Kody Dasher autonomous serving robots featuring 3-tiered anti-spill food trays, optical collision sensors. Voice-assisted customer table interaction.

Engineering and Delivery Workflow. Specifically, The restaurant floor is mapped in two hours using Dasher’s top-mounted LiDAR scanner. Tables are assigned digital coordinate tags (e.g., Table 1 to 45). Kitchen expediters place freshly plated dishes onto Dasher’s trays, input the destination table numbers via a capacitive touchscreen interface. Press 'Dispatch'. Dasher navigates aisles at 0.8 meters per second, dynamically steering around wandering children and moving chairs. Upon arrival, visual and voice prompts alert guests to collect their food, after which Dasher automatically returns to the kitchen staging station or parks at an induction charging dock.

Economics and ROI. Specifically, Dasher is sold for roughly ₹8–10 lakh ($10,000–$12,000) per unit or leased on a 36-month Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) contract at ₹30,000–35,000 per month. By substituting for two full-time runner positions (totaling ₹40,000 monthly in loaded wages, uniforms. Meals), the restaurant achieves cash-flow parity within month one and full capital payback within 22 to 24 months. Meanwhile, human servers are redeployed to higher-value guest hospitality and order upselling.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 3: Athena Autonomous Security & Perimeter Patrol at Tuneland Music Festival
paragraphs: Customer and Problem. Specifically, The organizers of Tuneland Music Festival 2024, hosting over 35,000 attendees across a multi-acre outdoor festival ground, require 24/7 continuous surveillance of perimeter fences, backstage access gates. Dense crowd choke points where stationary CCTV cameras suffer from blind spots and human guards experience fatigue.

Bought Solution. Specifically, Kody Athena autonomous surveillance robots equipped with dual optical-thermal pan-tilt-zoom cameras, night-vision infrared illumination, automated boundary geofencing. Real-time incident broadcast links to the event security command center.

Operational Deployment. Specifically, Athena was deployed on pre-programmed continuous patrol loops around high-density zones. Using on-board computer vision algorithms, Athena autonomously detected unattended backpacks, identified individuals loitering near restricted staging perimeters. Monitored crowd density surges, automatically beaming live encrypted HD video streams and thermal alerts to the festival control room.

Commercial Model. Specifically, Provided under an enterprise event-security service agreement. This generated direct high-margin demonstration and deployment fees. Meanwhile, serving as a proven institutional field reference for permanent industrial campus deployments.

web_blocks.text: The second operating vertical—Enterprise Software & Digital Transformation—is Kody's original cash engine. While overshadowed by the robotics narrative, this division employs a dedicated bench of software engineers building bespoke cloud systems, Flutter mobile applications. Enterprise microservices. Crucially, this engineering talent forms the foundational software backbone for robotics development. Specifically, Kody OS (the proprietary fleet management and robot teleoperation operating system), mobile companion apps that allow restaurant managers to summon Dasher from an iPad. Also, cloud portals that aggregate Odigo's advertising metrics are all engineered internally by this software division. [2][8]

In total, Kody Technolab has successfully developed an integrated hardware-plus-software product ecosystem. Unlike pure hardware re-sellers that import finished Chinese units and rebrand them, Kody conducts its own PCB design, embedded firmware programming, SLAM navigation tuning. Chassis assembly in Gujarat. However, from an investment perspective, the economic profile of these products remains heavily front-loaded. Specifically, each commercial sale requires extensive custom demonstration, long client acceptance testing. Extended payment terms. This creates an operational friction that is reflected directly in the company's working capital metrics. [1][4][6]

book_paragraphs: To understand what Kody Technolab actually does, you and I must step onto the factory floor in Gandhinagar and trace how an idea becomes a physical, commercial machine. If you look at the company's marketing brochures, it is easy to get dazzled by glossy photographs of sleek robots gliding through airports. But an institutional investor does not buy marketing brochures; an institutional investor buys unit economics, bills of materials, and customer problem-solving reality.

Today, Kody operates two businesses under one corporate roof. The first, contributing roughly a third of revenue, is the legacy enterprise software consultancy. It is unglamorous work—building mobile applications in Flutter, writing backend APIs in Node.js, and integrating cloud databases for corporate clients in India and overseas. It generates steady 30% operating margins, gets paid on monthly invoices, and requires virtually no capital expenditure. More importantly, this software bench is the technical mother lode from which all of Kody's robotics software springs. Every algorithm that allows a robot to read a LiDAR point cloud, map a restaurant dining room, or broadcast video telemetry to a cloud server is written by these engineers.

The second business—now generating over two-thirds of consolidated sales—is Kody Robots. Here, the company designs, builds, and deploys autonomous machines across three primary commercial use cases: customer service and retail media (Odigo), hospitality food delivery (Dasher), and security surveillance (Athena). Take Odigo, for instance. Walk through the Dubai Mall or GITEX exhibition hall. A traditional billboard is fixed to a wall; shoppers walk past it without looking. Odigo, by contrast, is an interactive digital advertising kiosk on wheels. It moves through the crowd, plays high-definition video advertisements on twin vertical screens, and uses computer vision to detect whether a passing shopper is a man or a woman, an adult or a child, dynamically serving relevant advertisements. When a visitor touches the screen asking for directions to an electronics retailer, Odigo displays the map and offers to lead them there. That is not just a robot; it is mobile, programmatic digital-out-of-home advertising.

Now look at Dasher in a busy dining establishment. In an industry plagued by high waiter turnover and rising minimum wages, food runners spend 70% of their shifts walking back and forth between the kitchen hot-line and customer tables. Dasher eliminates that walking. The kitchen expediter loads four hot entrees onto Dasher’s trays, taps 'Table 14', and Dasher glides silently down the aisle, using its LiDAR sensors to weave around chairs and guests. It never drops a plate, never takes a sick day, and never complains about working a double shift. At ₹8 to ₹10 lakh per unit, or ₹35,000 a month on lease, the restaurant owner cuts their front-of-house payroll costs by half and achieves payback within two years.

Then consider Athena. At an outdoor concert like Tuneland or around an expansive chemical refinery perimeter, paying three shifts of human security guards to walk boundary fences in extreme heat or darkness is expensive, prone to lapses, and hazardous. Athena rolls along the perimeter on autonomous patrol loops, using thermal vision to spot heat signatures through dense brush or darkness, identifying unattended packages, and beaming real-time encrypted alerts to a central monitoring room. A single security operator can monitor five Athena robots across a massive facility, transforming perimeter defense into a scalable software-driven operation.

This product portfolio proves that Kody is not an empty shell or a mere distributor of foreign kits. It is a genuine indigenous engineering and assembly operation. But as you and I analyze these segments, we must keep one crucial institutional reality in mind: selling capital equipment to hotels, malls, and event organizers is fundamentally harder than selling software hours. Every sale requires weeks of proof-of-concept testing, customized floor mapping, on-site staff training, and milestone-based payment schedules. In the next chapter, we will follow exactly how these machines are sold, delivered, and collected on the balance sheet.

Let us spend a moment examining the mechanical and software anatomy of these machines, because the boundary between hardware and software is where true value is created. Take Dasher, the hospitality robot. When you watch Dasher navigate a crowded restaurant dining room, what you are seeing is an intricate symphony of sensor fusion. Mounted near the base is a solid-state LiDAR unit that sweeps a 2D laser plane across the floor, measuring distances to tables, walls, and chair legs at thousands of points per second. Complementing the LiDAR are optical depth cameras mounted higher on the chassis, which detect overhangs, tabletop edges, and obstacles that sit above the laser sweep line.

All of this raw sensor telemetry is fed into an embedded computing unit running Kody OS. The operating software runs real-time Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms, matching the incoming laser point cloud against a pre-recorded digital floorplan of the restaurant. When a wandering customer steps into Dasher's path, the software cannot afford a two-second latency pause; it must re-calculate an alternate clearance trajectory in milliseconds, smoothly decelerating the brushless DC hub motors while maintaining the stability of the food trays above. Engineering that level of graceful, dependable motion is what separates an industrial-grade service robot from an amateur hobby project.

Now consider Odigo in the retail environment. In a bustling shopping mall concourse, Odigo is performing three distinct tasks simultaneously. First, it is an autonomous mobile vehicle navigating safely through dense pedestrian traffic without colliding with strollers, shopping bags, or running toddlers. Second, it is an interactive digital kiosk: when a shopper approaches, the robot uses facial detection algorithms to gauge attention, activating a high-definition touch display that allows the user to search for store locations, view promotional coupons, or request directions. Third, and most importantly from an economic perspective, Odigo is an intelligent programmatic advertising node. It logs impression data, records dwell times, and transmits encrypted telemetry back to the media network's cloud servers, providing advertisers with auditable metrics that traditional static billboards could never deliver.

Then look at Athena in perimeter security. Outdoor environments are vastly more demanding than air-conditioned shopping malls. An outdoor patrol robot must contend with rain, dust, gravel, temperature extremes, and uneven terrain. Athena's chassis is sealed against environmental ingress, and its sensor suite incorporates long-range thermal cameras capable of detecting human body heat in pitch darkness or through light foliage. When Athena patrols an industrial perimeter, it is executing an autonomous security route that would otherwise require three shifts of human guards. When an anomaly is detected—such as an open gate, an unrecognized thermal signature, or an unattended package—Athena triggers an alert directly to the central security monitoring console, beaming high-definition video so human supervisors can make an informed tactical intervention.

This detailed engineering walkthrough demonstrates that Kody has built genuine, functional, high-utility machines. However, an institutional investor must always link product capability back to customer economics. Does an airport or a mall operator view Odigo as an indispensable utility that they cannot operate without, or as a discretionary promotional asset that is easily cut when corporate budgets tighten? In hospitality, will restaurant owners continue to lease Dasher if food inflation compresses restaurant margins? These are the real-world demand questions that will determine whether Kody's segment revenues represent durable recurring cash flows or episodic novelty purchases.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Kody's product suite addresses genuine real-world friction: high labor turnover in hospitality, banner blindness in retail advertising, and human guard fatigue in perimeter security. The engineering execution is credible. The analytical question is whether customers treat these machines as mission-critical enterprise capital equipment or as discretionary promotional expenditure that gets slashed during economic downturns.
